newsitem.title: UK: Australian bonds lead field in past week -Salomon.
newsitem.headline: Australian bonds lead field in past week -Salomon.

text.p: Australian bonds easily outshined the rest of the pack amid mainly positive returns on government bonds for the past week, Salomon Brothers data showed on Friday.
The bank's world government bond index rose by 0.25 percent in the week to October 24 in local currency terms.

Benign inflation and wages data helped to push returns on Australian bonds to 1.38 percent. The data refuelled expectations of an early interest rate cut, sending yields on 10-year bonds to a 32-month low on Thursday.

An actual rate cut in Italy, where the discount rate fell to 7.5 percent from 8.25 percent, and recession fears over the budget helped Italian bonds to score returns of 1.04 percent, making them runners-up in the 16-country league table.

Japan came in third with a return of 0.83 percent, helped by a report that the Japanese Finance Ministry's Trust Fund Bureau would maintain its current portfolio strategy, which puts the heaviest weighting on JGBs (Japanese Government Bonds).

Japan was the only one of the big three world bond markets to manage positive returns. U.S. Treasuries had negative returns of 0.09 percent and German Bunds lost 0.06 percent, which was the third worst performance of all.
British gilts were the worst performers. They lost 0.21 percent in local currency terms, dragged down by Bunds and a slide in sterling.
It was a good week for European high yielders. As well as Italy, both Sweden and Spain were among the top half-dozen performers with returns of 0.75 percent and 0.43 percent, respectively.
Canada finished fifth with returns of 0.46 percent, while French bonds gained 0.17 percent.

New Zealand, which is not in the world bond index, came in even better than Australia with returns of 1.73 percent, against a background of a soaring currency and a central bank statement that monetary conditions were tighter than necessary.
In dollar terms, Sweden did best with returns of 1.90 percent, followed by Italy with 1.87 percent and Spain with 1.84 percent. France came next with 1.62 percent.
Apart from the U.S., all countries in the index had positive returns in dollar terms. The least impressive were Britain with 0.09 percent, Japan with 0.19 percent and Switzerland with 0.95 percent.

Salomon's bond index is calculated using all government bonds with more than one year to maturity, weighted for market capitalisation. Only bonds freely available to institutional investors and with a certain minimum amount outstanding are included. Returns take account of price moves and accrued interest.
